title: Teach someone the way
hookLine: hand on what you received, as Paul did
tomorrow: what do you sing when the whole journey is done?

lines: SOMEBODY KNELT DOWN AND SHOWED YOU.
cards: Nobody remembers learning to tie their shoes. Somebody knelt down, slowly, more than once, until the loop held.
Prayers usually come the same way: a grandmother at bedtime, a parent in a car, a hand guiding your hand from forehead to chest. Paul has a line about this that holds an odd detail.
Writing to Corinth about the Last Supper, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you." Received of the Lord. But Paul wasn't at that supper.
So who knelt down and showed him?

teach.b: Readers answer the puzzle two ways. Some hear it as direct: Paul tells the Galatians he received the gospel by a revelation of Jesus Christ.
Others hear it as a chain: the words came from the Lord, through those who were at the table, down to Paul. Either way, look at the two verbs. Received.
He uses them again a few chapters later, about the resurrection: "For I delivered unto you first of all, which I also received." Those are hand-to-hand words.
Nobody in this picture invents the faith; each one takes it, and passes it along.

teach.h: THE CHURCH HANDS ON WHAT SHE IS.
teach.b: Catholics call that living handing-on Tradition, and the Catechism describes it as the way the Church passes on all that she is and all that she believes, to every generation.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Last Supper reached the Corinthians the way your first prayer reached you, from somebody's hands.

teach.h: THE CHAIN HAS A SPARE LINK.
teach.b: And now the chain has a spare link.
Yours. Teaching the way doesn't mean a lecture. It can be one prayer, said slowly beside someone, the way it was said beside you.

how: Catholic parents, grandparents and godparents teach children the Sign of the Cross and first prayers at home; the Church calls the passing on of the faith Tradition.

games.q: what does “teach someone the way” mean?
o: become a teacher of religion at a school
explain the whole Catechism to a friend
pass the faith along the way it came to you

games.q: hand to hand — tap the pairs.
p: received of the Lord, delivered to you
the Church hands on what she is

s: Paul was at the Last Supper
he wasn't one of the Twelve at the table; he says he received it and delivered it.
Paul uses received and delivered again about the resurrection
"For I delivered unto you first of all, which I also received."
for Catholics, Tradition means old customs that never change
the Catechism describes it as a living handing-on of all the Church is and believes.

games.q: your seven-year-old nephew asks how to pray, and you've got two minutes before his ride comes. what's the move Paul's verbs point to?
o: explain what prayer means first, so he understands.
pray one short prayer slowly beside him, and let him copy.
find him a kids' prayer video to watch later.
games.why: received and delivered are hand-to-hand words. the faith reached Paul, and the Corinthians, from person to person; one prayer beside someone is the chain.

practice: Make the Sign of the Cross slowly, out loud, as if a child were copying you: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
Do it once more, slower, and let the sit hold the stillness after.

wordCard.voice: Teach someone the way. What Paul received, he delivered: one prayer, one person, hand to hand.

orig.note: Greek: I handed on, I delivered. Paul's verb in 1 Corinthians 11:23 and 15:3.

carryVoice: Carry this: hand it on, the way somebody once knelt down and showed you. Talk tomorrow.
